newsitem.title: USA: Falling US deficit guesses may lead to budget pact.
newsitem.headline: Falling US deficit guesses may lead to budget pact.

text.p: Much higher than anticipated income tax inflows could drive the U.S. budget deficit low enough to enable Republicans and Democrats to reach a compromise on a balanced budget within weeks, Wall Street experts said.

"Tax flows are coming in stronger than expected. It's still a little early to tell as the (Internal Revenue Service) is still processing checks, but I'd conservatively say the federal budget deficit will only be $75 billion," said James Glassman, senior economist at Chase Securities Inc.
There was a strong possibility the fiscal 1997 deficit would only be in the mid-$60 billion area, he added.
The Federal Reserve has had to execute multiple reserve adding operations in recent days because tax payments have been so high, Glassman said.
The Fed entered the open market on Monday morning via a round of three-day system repurchase agreements.

This has created a "double whammy" for the repurchase agreement market because the Treasury has been cutting the size of bill auctions in recent weeks -- creating a shortage of collateral at the same time the Fed has had the task of putting money back into the banking system.

But for politicians on both sides of the aisle, the huge inflows of tax payments were making it ideologically easier to strike a compromise. With a budget deficit potentially half the size of last year's, Democrats could wring out a lot less entitlement losses and Republicans stood to get tax break concessions.
"The job that needs to get done becomes so much smaller that it's enough to avoid tough decisions," Glassman said. "It lowers the hurdle for the job that needs to get done."

Timing was also a factor, as both parties could get political mileage out of a quickly reached agreement, Glassman said. There were still five months left in fiscal 1997 and an economic slowdown could lower tax collections and drive deficit projections higher. While any budget accord was bound to be a positive for the bond market, any sustainable gains would only come about if realistic budget cutting measures were enacted, economists said.

"It does lower the trajectory of growth for the expenditure side of the ledger. And there's no doubt that non-withheld tax payments were truly huge in April," said Kevin Flanagan, vice president and money market economist at Dean Witter Reynolds Inc.

But a lower deficit still didn't address the issue of tax cuts -- something the conservatives in Congress will be insistent upon, he added. In addition, there was a huge constituency of people who would object strongly to a more realistic reading of the consumer price index -- a key to trimming expenditures, he said.
"No doubt, initially the markets are going to like it (a budget accord). The question is how credible is it going to be?" Flanagan asked. "What type of restraints are going to be put on Congress?"
Treasury deposits at the Fed have shot higher, but Kim Rupert, senior economist at consulting firm MMS International Inc, said her firm is still expecting a deficit of $95 billion to $100 billion.
Rupert said given the strong economy and rising tax revenues, a budget accord could be expected within weeks.
"The economy remains in great shape and the deficit continues to decline. But we look to growth falling to a more sustainable 2.5 percent in the second half," said Rupert.
